text:
Before trusting any disease-association result, the pipeline first asked how much of the microbial compositional variance is explained by cohort of origin versus IBD status. The corresponding ordination confirms this visually: cohorts separate along PCoA1/PCoA2 far more clearly than IBD vs. control does within any single cohort (circle vs. triangle shapes are thoroughly intermixed within each cohort’s ellipse).






Figure 2: Bray-Curtis PCoA, species-level, colored by cohort and shaped by group. PCoA1 explains 15.6% of variance, PCoA2 9.3%. IjazUZ_2017 (green) is the most visually distinct cohort.



Practical consequence for everything downstream: the blocked Wilcoxon test explicitly blocks on cohort; both MaAsLin2 tiers include cohort as a random effect; and the ML validation strategy includes leave-one-cohort-out testing specifically because pooled cross-validation alone cannot rule out a model that has learned cohort identity rather than IBD biology.

section: 2 2. Alpha diversity: significant in species, not in pathway
text:
2 2. Alpha diversity: significant in species, not in pathway
Species-level alpha diversity is significantly reduced in IBD across all three metrics; pathway-level (functional) alpha diversity shows no significant difference — an important and genuine divergence between the taxonomic and functional layers, not an oversight.






Figure 3: Alpha diversity, species (top row) vs. pathway (bottom row). Species: richness p=0.0001, Shannon p<0.0001, Simpson p=0.0001 (Wilcoxon, unadjusted). Pathway: richness p=0.882, Shannon p=0.578, Simpson p=0.260 — none significant.

section: 3 3. Differential abundance: three independent tests, species vs. pathway
text:
3 3. Differential abundance: three independent tests, species vs. pathway
The species layer shows a strong, consistent differential-abundance signal across all three tests; the pathway layer shows a striking divergence between MaAsLin2 (almost no hits) and the blocked Wilcoxon test (many hits) — a finding worth featuring on its own.






Figure 4: Significant feature counts (q<0.05) out of total tested, species (blue) vs. pathway (orange), across all three DA tests.

Source: step8_maaslin2_tier1_hit_summary.csv, step9_maaslin2_tier2_hit_summary.csv, step12_wilcoxon_hit_summary.csv and pathway equivalents. The pathway MaAsLin2 models are effectively null (1/118 in both tiers) while the pathway blocked Wilcoxon test finds nearly half the tested pathways significant (52/118) — a large discrepancy between a mixed-model and a rank-based, cohort-blocked non-parametric test on the same data, worth treating as a genuine methodological finding rather than picking one number to report.

3.1 Species — Tier 1 and Tier 2 volcano plots






Figure 5: Species differential abundance, MaAsLin2 Tier 1 (all 353 samples). Gemmiger formicilis and Ruminococcus bromii are the two strongest depleted-in-IBD hits; Erysipelatoclostridium ramosum is the strongest enriched-in-IBD hit.









Figure 6: Species differential abundance, MaAsLin2 Tier 2 (age-adjusted subset, n=173). The same top hits (Gemmiger formicilis, Ruminococcus bromii, Adlercreutzia equolifaciens, Erysipelatoclostridium ramosum) remain significant after adjusting for age and restricting to the smaller age-available subset — direct evidence the Tier 1 signal is not simply an age confound.









Figure 7: Species differential abundance, cohort-blocked Wilcoxon test. Same top hits again — three independently-specified tests converge on the same leading species.





3.2 Pathway — blocked Wilcoxon significant features
Every one of the 52 pathways significant by the blocked Wilcoxon test is lower in IBD — no pathway shows significant enrichment. This one-directional pattern (loss of function, not gain) is consistent across nearly all detected pathways, in contrast to species, where both depletion and enrichment hits exist.






Figure 8: Pathways significant by blocked Wilcoxon (q<0.05), ranked by log₂ fold-change (IBD/control, cohort-blocked). All are depleted in IBD.





3.3 3-way convergence and the validated species signature
Requiring agreement across MaAsLin2 Tier 1, MaAsLin2 Tier 2, and the blocked Wilcoxon test — the pipeline’s core evidentiary bar — leaves 19 species as fully validated (“triple-candidates”), out of 65 Tier-1 hits.






Figure 9: 3-way overlap of species significance: MaAsLin2 Tier1, MaAsLin2 Tier2, and blocked Wilcoxon. 19 species pass all three tests; 29 pass Tier1+Wilcoxon but not the smaller-sample Tier2; only 2 pass Wilcoxon alone.



Of the 19 triple-candidates, 17 are depleted in IBD and 2 are enriched (Erysipelatoclostridium ramosum, [Clostridium] symbiosum) — both flagged as notable in Ning et al. 2023 as well (Ning et al. 2023). The signature is dominated by short-chain-fatty-acid-associated commensals (Gemmiger formicilis, Ruminococcus bromii, Fusicatenibacter saccharivorans, [Eubacterium] rectale).






Figure 10: The 19-species triple-candidate signature, ranked by log₂ fold-change, with prevalence in IBD vs. control shown alongside. Most depleted species (green) show markedly lower prevalence in IBD than in control; the two enriched species (orange) show the reverse pattern.



For reference, the full landscape of all 65 MaAsLin2-Tier1-significant species (i.e., before requiring 3-way agreement) is shown below — useful for seeing which additional species show a directionally consistent but less-replicated signal:






Figure 11: All 65 species significant in MaAsLin2 Tier 1, ranked by log₂ fold-change, with IBD/control prevalence bars.

A regularized linear model consistently beating three more flexible nonlinear ensembles, at n≈350 samples and 12–37 features, is itself a finding worth stating plainly: there isn’t enough data/signal in this regime for the trees’ extra flexibility to pay off, and L1/L2 regularization is doing real work.
Combining species and pathway barely improves over species alone (0.8313 vs. 0.8325 AUROC) despite more than doubling the feature count (37 vs. 17) — the added pathway features contribute little beyond what species already captures (confirmed independently by the SHAP analysis below).






Figure 13: ROC curves (mean ± 1 SD across 5 CV repeats) for the winning ElasticNet configuration per feature type. Real per-fold out-of-fold predictions (n=353 species / n=352 pathway & combined), not synthetic.









Figure 14: Precision-recall curves for the same three winning configurations, with baseline prevalence shown as a reference line.









Figure 15: Confusion matrices at the standard 0.5 probability threshold, one representative out-of-fold CV repeat per feature type.



The species classifier correctly identifies 192/217 IBD subjects (88% sensitivity) and 82/136 controls (60% specificity) at the default threshold; the pathway classifier’s much lower ceiling is visible directly in its confusion matrix (71% of true controls misclassified as IBD).

title: Results
text:
6 6. Leave-one-cohort-out (LOCO) validation
Pooled cross-validation cannot rule out a model that has learned cohort identity rather than disease biology — precisely the failure mode the PERMANOVA result (§1) warns is plausible here. LOCO trains on three cohorts and tests entirely on the fourth, held-out cohort (ElasticNet, rfe_full_pool panel, per feature type — note this is not necessarily each feature type’s pooled-CV winning panel, since species’ pooled winner was rfe_optimum; LOCO fixes rfe_full_pool across all three feature types for a controlled comparison).






Figure 16: LOCO AUROC by held-out cohort and feature type. Dashed line = chance (0.5). Single train/test split per cohort — no repeat variance is available (unlike the paper convention of n=5 repeated LOCO runs), so no error bars are shown; this is a real limitation of the current LOCO setup, not an omission.

title: Results
text:
7 7. Model interpretability: SHAP
SHAP values are available only for the combined model (species+pathway, 37 features, n=352) — no separate SHAP run exists per feature type.






Figure 17: Top-20 SHAP feature importances, combined ElasticNet model. Red = high (CLR-transformed) feature value, blue = low. Positive SHAP value pushes the prediction toward IBD.



Species features dominate the combined model’s predictions: 88.3% of total |SHAP| mass comes from species features, versus 11.7% from pathway features (combined_shap_contribution_by_type.csv) — direct, model-internal confirmation of the near-zero benefit from adding pathway features observed in the AUROC comparison above (§5). The six highest-ranked SHAP features (Adlercreutzia equolifaciens, Gemmiger formicilis, Ruminococcus bromii, [Ruminococcus] torques, Alistipes putredinis, [Clostridium] leptum) are all members of the 19-species triple-candidate signature identified independently by the statistical DA pipeline (§3) — convergence between an ML model’s learned feature importances and an independently-validated statistical signature, obtained via entirely different methodology, is the strongest piece of corroborating evidence in this project.

title: Results
text:
8 8. Summary: convergent evidence
Putting the independent lines of evidence side by side:

Statistical DA (3-way MaAsLin2×2 + blocked Wilcoxon convergence): 19 validated species
RFE (rfe_optimum, cross-validated AUROC-maximizing subset of those 19): 17 species
SHAP (combined ElasticNet’s top-ranked features): top 6 are all triple-candidates
ML performance: the RFE-optimum 17-species ElasticNet panel achieves 0.8325 AUROC pooled, and 0.71–0.96 AUROC across all four LOCO held-out cohorts

Three independently-specified statistical tests, an independent feature-selection procedure, and a fully independent nested-CV/Optuna-tuned classifier trained without any knowledge of the DA results all converge on substantially the same small set of species — Gemmiger formicilis, Ruminococcus bromii, Adlercreutzia equolifaciens, Alistipes putredinis foremost among them. That convergence, more than any single AUROC number, is this project’s central empirical result.

title: Methods
text: Methods are presented in the order the pipeline actually runs them: exploratory/confounder characterization → differential abundance (three independent tests) → feature selection → machine learning. Code snippets are pulled verbatim (trimmed for length) from the actual scripts in scripts/r/ and scripts/python/ — not rewritten.

title: Methods
text:
1 Part 1 — Statistical methods

1.1 Beta diversity: PERMANOVA on Bray-Curtis dissimilarity
Before drawing any disease-association conclusion, the pipeline explicitly quantifies how much of the compositional variance is attributable to cohort of origin versus IBD status, using vegan::adonis2 with marginal (by = "margin") term testing so each term’s R² reflects its contribution after accounting for the other. A base model (cohort + group) is run on all samples, then three covariate-adjusted submodels (+ age, + gender, + BMI) are run on the subset of cohorts where that covariate is actually available.
bray_dist <- vegdist(abund_matrix, method = "bray")
permanova_basic <- adonis2(bray_dist ~ cohort + group,
                            data = meta_for_permanova,
                            permutations = 999, by = "margin")

run_covariate_permanova <- function(covariate, cohorts_with_covariate) {
  d <- pooled_data %>% filter(cohort %in% cohorts_with_covariate, !is.na(.data[[covariate]]))
  bray_sub <- vegdist(as.matrix(d[, taxa_cols]), method = "bray")
  formula_str <- paste("bray_sub ~ cohort + group +", covariate)
  adonis2(as.formula(formula_str), data = d[, meta_cols], permutations = 999, by = "margin")
}
Source: scripts/r/04_diversity_permanova.R (species) / 14_pathway_diversity_permanova.R (pathway).


1.2 Alpha diversity: Wilcoxon rank-sum + cohort-adjusted LME
Alpha diversity (Shannon, Simpson, observed richness) is computed on the full raw abundance table (pre-filtering, deliberately — filtering thresholds are tuned for differential-abundance testing, not diversity estimation), then tested two ways: an unadjusted Wilcoxon rank-sum test (IBD vs. control, pooled), and a linear mixed-effects model with cohort as a random intercept (nlme::lme), to check whether the unadjusted result survives accounting for cohort clustering.
shannon_idx <- diversity(abund_matrix, index = "shannon")
wilcox_shannon <- wilcox.test(shannon ~ group, data = diversity_df)
lme_shannon <- lme(shannon ~ group, random = ~1|cohort, data = diversity_df)
Source: scripts/r/04_diversity_permanova.R, lines 82–117.


1.3 Differential abundance, Tier 1: MaAsLin2 (all samples)
MaAsLin2 (Mallick et al. 2021) is run with group (control vs. IBD) as a fixed effect and cohort as a random effect, on the full sample set. TSS normalization, log transform, linear-model backend, BH FDR correction (config.yaml: maaslin2). control is explicitly releveled as the reference so a positive coefficient means enriched in IBD.
input_metadata$group <- relevel(factor(input_metadata$group), ref = "control")

fit_tier1 <- Maaslin2(
  input_data      = input_data,
  input_metadata  = input_metadata,
  fixed_effects   = c("group"),
  random_effects  = c("cohort"),
  normalization   = "TSS",
  transform       = "LOG",
  analysis_method = "LM",
  correction      = "BH",
  standardize     = TRUE
)
Source: scripts/r/06_maaslin2_tier1.R.


1.4 Differential abundance, Tier 2: MaAsLin2 (age-adjusted subset)
A robustness check on the subset of cohorts/subjects with non-missing age (covariate_availability.rds, derived empirically from the data rather than hardcoded — see the reproducibility caveat on the Data & Cohort page), adding age as a second fixed effect alongside group.
fit_tier2 <- Maaslin2(
  input_data      = input_data_t2,
  input_metadata  = input_metadata_t2,
  fixed_effects   = c("group", "age"),
  random_effects  = c("cohort"),
  normalization   = "TSS", transform = "LOG",
  analysis_method = "LM",  correction = "BH",
  standardize     = TRUE
)
tier2_group_results <- fit_tier2$results %>% filter(metadata == "group")
Source: scripts/r/07_maaslin2_tier2_age.R. Note: plot_scatter=FALSE is set in both tiers as a workaround for a MaAsLin2/ggplot2 version incompatibility in its continuous-covariate scatter-plot code (confirmed via log: model fit and $results extraction are unaffected).


1.5 Differential abundance, blocked Wilcoxon test
An independent, non-parametric test: a cohort-blocked Wilcoxon rank-sum test (coin::wilcox_test, block = cohort, conditional/permutation-based null distribution), run separately per feature. coin’s raw test statistic does not follow MaAsLin2’s “positive = enriched in IBD” sign convention, so the pipeline flips the sign and empirically verifies the correction against real group medians before trusting it (hard stopifnot, not just a comment):
wt <- coin::wilcox_test(abundance ~ group | cohort, data = df, distribution = "asymptotic")
statistic_corrected <- -as.numeric(coin::statistic(wt))

# Empirical verification, not assumed:
ibd_higher <- medians_check$median_abund[medians_check$group == "IBD"] >
              medians_check$median_abund[medians_check$group == "control"]
corrected_positive <- corrected_stat > 0
stopifnot(ibd_higher == corrected_positive)  # hard stop if the sign convention doesn't hold
Source: scripts/r/09_species_wilcoxon.R. FDR correction: BH, same threshold (q < 0.05) as MaAsLin2.


1.6 3-way convergent feature selection (“triple-candidates”)
A feature is only trusted if all three tests agree: MaAsLin2 Tier 1 (q < 0.05) ∩ MaAsLin2 Tier 2 (q < 0.05) ∩ blocked Wilcoxon (q < 0.05) — then a direction-agreement check (MaAsLin2 coefficient sign vs. corrected Wilcoxon statistic sign) — then a third, independent effect-size check using generalized fold change (gFC), a quantile-based, non-parametric fold-change estimate robust to zero-inflation:
compute_gfc <- function(x, group, q_range) {
  x_ibd <- x[group == "IBD"]; x_control <- x[group == "control"]
  pc <- min(x[x > 0], na.rm = TRUE) / 2
  q_ibd     <- quantile(log10(x_ibd + pc), probs = q_range, na.rm = TRUE)
  q_control <- quantile(log10(x_control + pc), probs = q_range, na.rm = TRUE)
  mean(q_ibd - q_control)
}
# q_range: seq(0.1, 0.9, 0.05) -- config.yaml: gfc.quantile_range

triple_candidates$gfc_maaslin_agree <- sign(triple_candidates$gFC) == sign(triple_candidates$coef_maaslin_tier1)
triple_candidates$gfc_wilcox_agree  <- sign(triple_candidates$gFC) == sign(triple_candidates$statistic_wilcox_corrected)
Only features passing the intersection, the direction check, and the gFC agreement check on both other tests survive as “triple-candidates.” Source: scripts/r/10_species_triple_candidates.R (mirrored for pathway in 19_pathway_triple_candidates.R). Results: 19 species and 18 pathways survived this full pipeline (see Results).

title: Methods
section: 2 Part 2 — Feature selection: Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE)
text:
2 Part 2 — Feature selection: Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE)
The triple-candidate pool (19 species / 18 pathways) is further reduced via Recursive Feature Elimination (caret::rfe), random-forest-based, AUC-optimized (twoClassSummary), 10-fold CV, producing a cross-validated AUROC-vs-panel-size curve. Three panels are derived from each curve:

rfe_optimum — the panel size with the single best cross-validated AUROC (which.max(results_df$ROC))
rfe_parsimony — the smallest panel within 1% tolerance of the optimum (caret::pickSizeTolerance(..., tol = 1))
rfe_full_pool — the entire triple-candidate pool, unranked, as an upper-bound reference

rfe_result <- rfe(x = feat_matrix, y = y, sizes = 2:n_candidates,
                   rfeControl = ctrl_auc, metric = "ROC")

optimum_size   <- results_df$Variables[which.max(results_df$ROC)]
parsimony_size <- caret::pickSizeTolerance(results_df, metric = "ROC", tol = 1, maximize = TRUE)
Source: scripts/r/11_species_rfe.R, lines 68–97 (mirrored in 20_pathway_rfe.R). Panel design explicitly credited to the RFE-to-a-compact-panel approach used in Ning et al. 2023, Zheng et al. 2024, and Zhou et al. 2024 (script header comment). Resulting panel sizes: species — 12 / 17 / 19; pathway — 9 / 12 / 18 (see Results).

title: Methods
text:
3 Part 3 — Machine learning

3.1 Feature transform: centered log-ratio (CLR)
Before any modeling, the full filtered feature table (151 species or 118 pathways — not yet subset to an RFE panel) is CLR-transformed. This ordering matters: CLR is not sub-compositionally coherent, so computing it on a pre-cut panel would use the wrong geometric-mean reference; panel subsetting always happens after CLR, never before.
def clr_transform(df, pseudocount_method="half_min_nonzero"):
    values = df.values.astype(float)
    pseudocount = values[values > 0].min() / 2
    log_vals = np.log(values + pseudocount)
    row_means = log_vals.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    clr_vals = log_vals - row_means
    clr_df = pd.DataFrame(clr_vals, index=df.index, columns=df.columns)
    assert clr_df.sum(axis=1).abs().max() < 1e-6  # CLR rows must sum to ~0
    return clr_df, pseudocount
Source: scripts/python/utils/cv_utils.py, lines 39–80.


3.2 Nested cross-validation with Bayesian hyperparameter search
Every model/panel combination is evaluated with the same nested-CV engine: an outer loop of RepeatedStratifiedKFold (10 splits × 5 repeats = 50 outer folds, random_state=123) provides untouched held-out test folds; for each outer training fold, an inner Optuna study (TPE sampler, 5-fold StratifiedKFold, 30 trials, optimizing mean inner-fold ROC AUC) searches hyperparameters; the best inner configuration is refit on the full outer-training fold and evaluated once on its untouched outer-test fold.
outer_cv = RepeatedStratifiedKFold(n_splits=10, n_repeats=5, random_state=123)
for fold_num, (train_idx, test_idx) in enumerate(outer_cv.split(X_arr, y_arr)):
    def objective(trial):
        model = get_model_for_trial(trial, model_name)
        inner_cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=123)
        scores = [roc_auc_score(y_train[val], model.fit(X_train[tr], y_train[tr]).predict_proba(X_train[val])[:, 1])
                  for tr, val in inner_cv.split(X_train, y_train)]
        return float(np.mean(scores))

    study = optuna.create_study(direction="maximize", sampler=optuna.samplers.TPESampler(seed=123))
    study.optimize(objective, n_trials=30)
    final_model = get_model_for_trial(study.best_params, model_name).fit(X_train, y_train)
    y_proba = final_model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
Per-repeat metrics are computed by averaging the 10 fold-level metrics within each repeat — never by pooling raw fold rows together, which would pseudo-replicate the confidence interval:
def aggregate_per_repeat(fold_results_df, n_splits):
    df = fold_results_df.copy()
    df["repeat_id"] = df["fold_num"] // n_splits
    metric_cols = ["auroc", "auprc", "sensitivity", "specificity", "precision", "f1", "accuracy"]
    return df.groupby("repeat_id")[metric_cols].mean().reset_index()
Source: scripts/python/utils/cv_utils.py, run_nested_cv_optuna() (lines 187–299) and aggregate_per_repeat() (lines 99–109).


3.3 Model families
Four model families are evaluated on every feature panel, so the model choice is empirically justified rather than assumed — following the same “sweep several algorithms, don’t presuppose a winner” discipline used in Zhou et al. 2024’s CRC/CRA screen:

Sweep scope: species — 4 models × 3 panels = 12 runs; pathway — 4 models × 3 panels = 12 runs; combined (species + pathway concatenated post-CLR, species__/pathway__ prefixed) — 4 models × 1 fixed panel (rfe_full_pool, 37 features) = 4 runs. 28 nested-CV runs total.


3.4 Evaluation metrics
AUROC and AUPRC are the primary metrics (via roc_auc_score/average_precision_score on held-out fold predictions); sensitivity, specificity, precision, F1, and accuracy are also logged per fold at a 0.5 probability threshold. All metrics, per-repeat values, and raw out-of-fold predictions (y_true/y_proba) are logged as MLflow artifacts for every run.


3.5 Leave-one-cohort-out (LOCO) validation
Pooled cross-validation cannot detect a classifier that has learned cohort identity rather than disease biology — a real risk given the PERMANOVA finding that cohort explains far more compositional variance than IBD status (see Results). LOCO directly tests this: train on three cohorts, evaluate on the entirely held-out fourth cohort, repeated for each of the four cohorts. Unlike the pooled sweep, LOCO runs ElasticNet only, on the rfe_full_pool panel, for each feature type — a single train/test split per held-out cohort (not repeated), with its own 20-trial Optuna inner search on the training cohorts.
for held_out_cohort in cohorts:
    train_mask = data["cohort"] != held_out_cohort
    test_mask  = data["cohort"] == held_out_cohort
    scaler = StandardScaler()  # fit on TRAINING cohorts only -- no leakage from held-out cohort
    X_train = scaler.fit_transform(X_train_raw); X_test = scaler.transform(X_test_raw)

    study = optuna.create_study(direction="maximize", sampler=optuna.samplers.TPESampler(seed=123))
    study.optimize(objective, n_trials=20)
    final_model = LogisticRegression(**study.best_params, penalty="elasticnet", solver="saga").fit(X_train, y_train)
    y_proba = final_model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
Source: scripts/python/06_loco_validation.py.


3.6 Model interpretability: SHAP
SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) (Lundberg and Lee 2017) values are computed for the combined feature type’s winning ElasticNet model only (scripts/python/05_combined_shap.py) — no separate SHAP run exists for species-only or pathway-only models. LinearExplainer is used on the final refit ElasticNet, giving exact (not sampled/approximate) attributions consistent with the model’s linear decision function.


3.7 Statistical comparison of models
Pairwise model comparisons (e.g., ElasticNet vs. each tree ensemble, within a panel) use both a paired t-test and a paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test across the 5 per-repeat metric values. With only n = 5 paired repeats, Wilcoxon’s exact p-value floors at 0.0625 regardless of effect size — this is called out explicitly in the pipeline’s own output (wilcoxon_underpowered_at_n5 flag column) rather than silently reported, and the paired t-test is used as the primary significance criterion for this reason.
Source: scripts/python/07_statistical_comparison.py.

title: Background
text:
Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) — comprising Crohn’s disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC) — is a chronic relapsing inflammatory condition of the gastrointestinal tract, currently diagnosed through invasive endoscopic and histological workup. Over the past decade, shotgun metagenomic sequencing of stool has repeatedly shown that gut microbial community composition differs systematically between IBD patients and healthy individuals, motivating interest in the gut microbiome as a non-invasive diagnostic signal.
A persistent obstacle to translating that observation into a usable diagnostic tool is cross-cohort inconsistency: microbial signatures discovered in one study population frequently fail to reproduce in another, because cohort of origin (sequencing center, geography, diet, DNA extraction protocol) is itself a strong driver of microbiome composition — often stronger than disease status. Any classifier trained naively on pooled data risks learning cohort identity rather than disease biology.
This project builds an end-to-end, reproducible Snakemake pipeline that:

Pools four independently collected, publicly available IBD metagenomic cohorts from curatedMetagenomicData (Pasolli et al. 2017),
Explicitly tests for and accounts for cohort-driven compositional variance before drawing any disease-association conclusions,
Identifies differentially abundant taxa and functional pathways using three independent statistical approaches, requiring agreement across all three before a feature is trusted, and
Builds and rigorously cross-validates machine-learning classifiers — including a leave-one-cohort-out (LOCO) generalization test — to evaluate whether the resulting microbial signature can distinguish IBD from non-IBD gut microbiomes in samples the model has never seen.

text:

Explicitly tests for and accounts for cohort-driven compositional variance before drawing any disease-association conclusions,
Identifies differentially abundant taxa and functional pathways using three independent statistical approaches, requiring agreement across all three before a feature is trusted, and

title: Background
text:
2 Why this design
The analysis design is directly inspired by three published cross-cohort microbiome-ML studies made available alongside this project (see ML-ibd/*.pdf):

Ning et al. 2023, Nature Communications (Ning et al. 2023) — cross-cohort integrative analysis (CCIA) of 9 metagenomic IBD cohorts, combining differential abundance testing across cohorts with random-forest diagnostic models validated via cohort-to-cohort transfer and leave-one-cohort-out (LOCO) analysis. This project’s overall structure — pool cohorts, test for cohort effects, screen features for cross-cohort consistency, then validate with LOCO — mirrors this paper’s workflow directly.
Zhou et al. 2024, Frontiers in Molecular Biosciences (Zhou et al. 2024) — cross-cohort feature screening for colorectal cancer/adenoma diagnosis, using SHAP-based feature intersection across cohorts and comparison of multiple ML algorithms (XGBoost, LightGBM, Random Forest, Logistic Regression, SVM, k-NN) before selecting a final model family. This project’s model sweep (four algorithm families evaluated per feature panel, described in Methods) follows the same “don’t assume one model wins” discipline.
Zheng et al. 2024, Nature Medicine (Zheng et al. 2024) — noninvasive, microbiome-based diagnosis of IBD, motivating the overall clinical framing: can gut microbiome composition alone, without endoscopy, support an IBD vs. non-IBD screening decision.

title: Background
text:
3 Clinical / scientific question
Given fecal shotgun metagenomic species- and pathway-level abundance profiles pooled across four independent cohorts, can gut microbiome composition distinguish individuals with IBD from non-IBD individuals, using a signature that is (a) statistically consistent across cohorts and (b) validated on cohorts the model was not trained on?






NoteScope: binary IBD vs. non-IBD, not CD vs. UC



The four cohorts pooled in this pipeline are labeled by disease status in curatedMetagenomicData’s sampleMetadata, which this project collapses to a binary IBD vs. control (non-IBD) group at the cohort-selection step (scripts/r/01_cohort_selection.R): samples coded "healthy" become control, and any sample whose disease field contains "IBD" becomes IBD. All statistical testing, differential abundance analysis, and machine-learning models in this project operate on that binary label — no CD-vs-UC subtype distinction is part of this analysis. Both Ning et al. and Zheng et al. note the same binary framing for their primary diagnostic models; Ning et al. additionally builds a separate, secondary CD-vs-UC sub-panel from a different, smaller feature set — this project does not attempt that secondary analysis, since subtype labels are not retained past the cohort-selection step here.

title: What We Tried To Do
text: Distinguish IBD from non-IBD (control) gut microbiome samples using cross-cohort, pooled shotgun metagenomic species and pathway abundance data, via machine-learning classifiers that are validated not just by pooled cross-validation but by explicit out-of-cohort generalization testing.

title: What We Tried To Do
text: Distinguish IBD from non-IBD (control) gut microbiome samples using cross-cohort, pooled shotgun metagenomic species and pathway abundance data, via machine-learning classifiers that are validated not just by pooled cross-validation but by explicit out-of-cohort generalization testing.

title: What We Tried To Do
text:
2 Specific aims

Characterize cohort structure before touching disease signal. Quantify how much of the variance in microbial community composition is explained by cohort of origin versus IBD status (PERMANOVA on Bray-Curtis dissimilarity), so that downstream conclusions can be interpreted against that baseline rather than assumed to be disease-specific.
Identify differentially abundant species and pathways between IBD and control, using three statistically independent methods — MaAsLin2 (all-samples model), MaAsLin2 (age-adjusted subset), and a cohort-blocked Wilcoxon rank-sum test — and require 3-way agreement plus direction agreement before treating a feature as a validated hit. This is deliberately conservative: any single test can produce false positives driven by one dominant cohort; requiring convergence across three differently-specified tests is the project’s main defense against that.
Characterize the pathway (functional) layer separately from the species (taxonomic) layer, since a priori it is not obvious that pathway-level function will show the same cross-cohort consistency as species-level composition — this project treats that as an empirical question, not an assumption, and the two layers are analyzed in fully parallel but independent tracks.
Reduce the validated feature sets to compact, ranked panels via Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE, random-forest-based, AUC-optimized), producing three panel sizes per feature type (species and pathway) that trade off predictive performance against parsimony.
Train and compare multiple ML model families (Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, ElasticNet-penalized Logistic Regression) on each feature panel, using nested cross-validation with Bayesian hyperparameter search, so that model choice — not just feature choice — is empirically justified rather than assumed.
Stress-test generalization with leave-one-cohort-out (LOCO) validation. Pooled cross-validation cannot detect a model that has learned cohort-specific rather than disease-specific signal; LOCO — training on three cohorts and testing entirely on a fourth, held out cohort — directly probes this failure mode, following the same design used in Ning et al. 2023 (Ning et al. 2023).
Interpret the winning model, using SHAP values to identify which individual features drive its predictions, and cross-reference those features against the independently validated differential-abundance signature — convergence between an ML model’s learned importances and an independent statistical test is stronger evidence than either alone.

title: What We Tried To Do
section: 3 What this project deliberately does not attempt
text:
3 What this project deliberately does not attempt

CD vs. UC subtyping — out of scope; see the Background callout on why.
Causal or mechanistic claims — this is a classification/association study on cross-sectional, pooled public cohorts; no claim is made about microbiome-driven causation of IBD.
Metabolomics or host transcriptomic integration — unlike Ning et al. 2023’s multi-omics design, this pipeline works from metagenomic species and pathway abundance only; no metabolomic layer is available in the source cohorts used here.
